nonScoring.title: Primary snapshot writer (pull-yahoo.js) never adopted the shared safeSnapshotFilename — drift surface the module exists to kill is still open
nonScoring.evidence: lib/snapshot-fs.js docstring claims it centralises the helper so 'future snapshot-naming changes need to land in exactly one file'. But pull-yahoo.js:38 still carries a PRIVATE verbatim copy: `function safeSnapshotFilename(ticker){ const sanitized = String(ticker).replace(/[^A-Z0-9.-]/gi,'_'); const stem = sanitized.split('.')[0]; if (WINDOWS_RESERVED.test(stem)) return '_'+sanitized+'.json'; return sanitized+'.json'; }` and even re-exports it (pull-yahoo.js:2352). The READERS (scripts/regional-oos-test.js:17, scripts/prune-watchlist.js:26, scripts/elliott-export.js:47) all import the shared lib version. So the file-naming contract is split across two definitions: the writer's private copy and the lib copy the readers trust.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: Snapshots are the spine of the pipeline (Yahoo -> snapshots -> scoring). The writer and the readers agreeing on the on-disk filename is a hard invariant. Today the two copies are byte-identical, so nothing breaks — but the entire reason F-218b-01 created lib/snapshot-fs.js was to remove exactly this drift surface, and it failed to migrate the one caller that matters most. A future edit to the writer's copy (e.g. adding a new reserved name, changing the sanitiser char class) silently desyncs writer from readers: pull-yahoo writes `_NEWRES.json`, regional-oos-test/elliott/prune look for `NEWRES.json`, and the ticker vanishes from OOS tests and exports with no error — the same silent-skip survivorship-attrition bug (CON -> _CON.json invisibility) the helper was created to fix, just relocated.
nonScoring.fix: Delete the private copy in pull-yahoo.js (lines 32-43) and `const { safeSnapshotFilename } = require('./lib/snapshot-fs.js');`. Keep the re-export in module.exports by re-exporting the imported symbol so pull-yahoo's own consumers are unaffected. Do NOT touch methods/index.js. This is the only remaining caller not on the shared helper; once migrated the drift surface is genuinely closed.

nonScoring.title: Windows reserved-name guard misses reserved stems that contain non-alphanumerics and the bare 'COM0'/extension-suffix cases; also fails the dot-as-first-char case
nonScoring.evidence: `const sanitized = String(ticker).replace(/[^A-Z0-9.-]/gi,'_'); const stem = sanitized.split('.')[0]; if (WINDOWS_RESERVED.test(stem)) return '_'+sanitized+'.json';` with `WINDOWS_RESERVED = /^(CON|PRN|AUX|NUL|COM[1-9]|LPT[1-9])$/i`. Two gaps: (1) the stem is taken as `split('.')[0]`, so a ticker like `CON_X` (a space/slash in the source ticker becomes `_`, giving stem `CON_X`) is NOT matched and is written as `CON_X.json` — but Windows only reserves the *exact* device names, so `CON_X` is actually safe; the real miss is the opposite: Windows ALSO reserves the device name when it appears as the full base name regardless of extension, which is handled, BUT it does NOT reserve `COM0`/`LPT0` — fine. (2) The genuinely missing modern reserved names: Windows also reserves `CONIN$`, `CONOUT$`, and on recent Windows the superscript COM/LPT digits, but more practically a ticker that is *only* a dot or starts with a dot (e.g. a malformed `.DE`) yields stem `''`, regex fails, file `.DE.json` — a hidden dotfile on POSIX and an odd name on Windows.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: This is the same class as the original CON.DE / Continental AG bug (Tag 134) that motivated the helper. The guard is a denylist of exact names; any ticker whose sanitised stem is a reserved device name written WITHOUT the helper-known form silently fails to write on Windows, breaking `git checkout`/`git pull` for Karl's Windows box and dropping that ticker's snapshot. Because the constraint forbids hardcoded ticker exclusions, the guard itself is the right place to harden.
nonScoring.fix: Tighten the guard rather than excluding tickers: after computing `stem`, also strip a trailing/leading dot and reject empty stems by prefixing `_`; and treat a stem that is empty or that case-insensitively equals a reserved name as reserved. Add the `CONIN$`/`CONOUT$` forms to WINDOWS_RESERVED. Each change carries a comment naming the failure mode: '// prevents un-writable snapshot on Windows (git checkout breaks) for reserved/empty stem'. Keep the regex anchored.

nonScoring.title: extractStocksArray and detectShape are exported but have zero importers — dead public surface
nonScoring.evidence: A repo-wide grep for `extractStocksArray|detectShape` returns only their own definitions (watchlist-fs.js:75,82), the docstring example (line 21), and the module.exports (line 108). The single real consumer of this module is scripts/check-pull-stats.js:36 which imports only `loadWatchlist`. No file imports `extractStocksArray` or `detectShape`.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: Dead exports widen the public API the maintainer must keep correct and tempt a future caller to wire up a thin wrapper that bypasses loadWatchlist's error contract (the {shape, stocks, size, raw, error} envelope). The internal `_classify` already centralises the logic; the two public wrappers add surface without a caller. Low risk today, but this module was itself created to *reduce* drift surface, so exporting unused variants works against that goal.
nonScoring.fix: Either drop `extractStocksArray` and `detectShape` from module.exports (keep `_classify` internal and `loadWatchlist` as the sole entrypoint) and remove them from the docstring, or add a one-line comment marking them as a deliberately-kept public API for external scripts. Given the module's stated single-source-of-truth purpose, prefer removing them.

nonScoring.title: Insurance industries misclassified as FINTECH; keyword branch swallows insurers before any insurance-specific or sector check
nonScoring.evidence: Line 89: `if (ind.includes('fintech') || ind.includes('payment') || ind.includes('insurance')) return SUB_PROFILES.FINTECH;`. There is no INSURANCE sub-profile, and insurers (industry strings like 'Insurance—Property & Casualty', 'Insurance—Life', 'Insurance Brokers') are routed to FINTECH. FINTECH carries `antiManipFilters: []` (line 23) — and even the SaaS/Hardware profiles that DO carry anti-manip filters wouldn't fit an insurer. An insurer's economics (float, combined ratio, reserves) are nothing like a payments/fintech name.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: sub-profile drives sector-relative scoring (methods/sector-relative-roic.js:119 calls H.classifySubProfile and buckets the stock). Lumping P&C/Life insurers into FINTECH pollutes the FINTECH peer-median used for relative ROIC/quality scoring: insurers have structurally different ROIC and margins, so both the insurers AND the genuine fintech names get a distorted peer baseline. This is a silent scoring-quality cap — exactly the kind of structural ceiling implied by 'screener at ~20% of potential'. It is data-driven (no ticker hardcoding) so it is in-bounds to fix.
nonScoring.fix: Route insurance to a more economically-honest bucket. Minimal fix without adding a profile: move insurers to BANK (closest balance-sheet-driven peer set) or FINTECH only for 'insurance brokers' (fee-based) while sending carriers elsewhere. Cleaner fix: add an INSURANCE sub-profile to SUB_PROFILES and branch on `ind.includes('insurance')` before line 89. Comment: '// prevents insurer float/combined-ratio economics from polluting the FINTECH peer-median used in sector-relative scoring'.

nonScoring.title: TICKER_SUBPROFILE_MAP is a hardcoded ticker override table baked into a 'pure deterministic classifier' — and it is exported but unused, so overrides silently depend on Yahoo meta.ticker exact-casing
nonScoring.evidence: Lines 33-56 hardcode ~22 ticker->profile overrides (NVDA->HARDWARE, META->MARKETPLACE, AAPL->HARDWARE, etc.). classifySubProfile reads `const ticker = (stock.meta && stock.meta.ticker || '').toUpperCase().trim();` (line 67) then `TICKER_SUBPROFILE_MAP[ticker]`. The map has both `RHM` and `RHM.DE` (lines 40-41) — duplicating the override for the regional suffix, which means any *other* dual-listed ticker (e.g. a US ADR vs local line) silently falls through to the heuristic for one of its two forms. TICKER_SUBPROFILE_MAP is also exported (line 120) but imported nowhere (grep: only engine-cli-tests imports classifySubProfile/SUB_PROFILES).
nonScoring.why_it_matters: (1) Correctness coupling: the override key is the post-uppercase Yahoo `meta.ticker`. If a snapshot stores the ticker with an exchange suffix (`META` vs `META.US`) or Yahoo changes casing, the override misses and the stock reverts to the heuristic — e.g. META falls out of MARKETPLACE into... the heuristic, which for 'Internet Content & Information' has no explicit branch and could land OTHER. This is a silent, per-ticker classification flip. (2) The map is a maintenance liability: a hand-curated allowlist of megacaps inside a 'pure, deterministic' library is the kind of thing that drifts as Yahoo industries change, and the comment on NVDA even admits 'User-Diskussion offen'. (3) Dead export widens surface.
nonScoring.fix: Do not remove the overrides (they encode real judgement calls) but: (a) drop TICKER_SUBPROFILE_MAP from module.exports since no one imports it; (b) normalise the lookup key to strip the exchange suffix (match on `ticker.split('.')[0]`) so RHM and RHM.DE need only one entry and dual-listings are robust — comment: '// prevents override-miss when Yahoo returns the suffixed ticker form, which silently reverts the stock to the keyword heuristic'; (c) consider moving the table to a data/config file long-term so the classifier stays pure. No hardcoded *exclusions* are involved, so this respects the constraint.

nonScoring.title: Comment/code mismatch on Discord retry_after units; relies on body field being seconds while the comment claims milliseconds
nonScoring.evidence: Line 116 comment: '429: honor retry-after (header in seconds, body in milliseconds).' Line 126: `if (j && Number.isFinite(j.retry_after)) waitMs = Math.max(waitMs, Math.ceil(j.retry_after * 1000));`. The code multiplies the JSON body's `retry_after` by 1000 (seconds->ms), which is correct for the actual Discord API (v8+ returns `retry_after` as a float in SECONDS, not ms). So the CODE is right but the COMMENT is wrong — the body is seconds, not milliseconds.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: The behaviour is currently correct (×1000 of a seconds value gives ms), so no live bug. But the misleading comment is a trap: a future maintainer trusting 'body in milliseconds' could 'fix' the apparent ×1000 by removing it, which would then under-wait by 1000× and reintroduce dropped 429 alerts under sustained rate-limiting — the exact failure F-230c-06 was added to prevent. Since picks-regression-check (the noisy-day burst path) depends on this, the latent foot-gun is worth removing.
nonScoring.fix: Correct the comment to 'header in seconds (integer), body retry_after in seconds (float)'. No code change. This keeps the alert-durability guarantee legible.

nonScoring.title: 429 retry consumes a loop iteration without counting toward a network-call budget; a 429+5xx mix can issue up to maxRetries+2 POSTs and a non-final 429 does not honor a body retry_after cap symmetrically
nonScoring.evidence: On a non-final 429 the code computes waitMs (capped 10s), sleeps, and `continue`s WITHOUT decrementing any separate budget (line 149-150). On the final attempt it does an EXTRA honored sleep+post (lines 136-148). So the worst-case POST count is the loop body (attempts 0..maxRetries = 3 posts) PLUS the terminal honored retry (1 more) = up to 4 network POSTs for maxRetries=2. Separately, a non-final 429 reads the body via _jsonWithTimeout (line 125) only on... it does read it on every 429 including non-final — but the `waitMs = Math.min(waitMs, 10000)` cap (line 130) is applied before the final-attempt branch, so the terminal honored retry also respects the 10s cap; that part is fine.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: This is defensive code for alert durability, so erring toward more retries is acceptable per the module's own rationale ('a true duplicate alert is far better than a missed one'). The only real concern is that the retry accounting is implicit: the loop variable doubles as both 'attempt index' and 'retry budget', so reasoning about the true maximum wall-clock (up to 3×timeout for posts + 2×10s sleeps + 1×500ms ≈ 35s) is non-obvious and could brush against a CI step timeout, the very thing the AbortController was added to bound. Low severity because each individual call is bounded.
nonScoring.fix: No behavioural change required, but add a one-line comment documenting the worst-case wall-clock (POSTs + honored sleeps) so the CI-timeout interaction is explicit, OR introduce an explicit `maxWallClockMs` guard if Karl wants a hard ceiling. Leave the dedupe-friendly extra retry as-is.

nonScoring.title: writeJsonAtomic serialises with JSON.stringify and no replacer guard — NaN/Infinity silently become null, corrupting numeric state files written through the 'safe' path
nonScoring.evidence: Line 172: `const payload = JSON.stringify(value, opts.replacer || null, indent);`. JSON.stringify converts NaN, Infinity and -Infinity to the literal `null`, and drops `undefined`-valued keys. This helper is the atomic writer used by fitness/measure.js:250 (`writeJsonAtomic(outFile, output)`) for computed fitness output, and the same JSON.stringify path is used implicitly by every writeFileAtomic caller that does `JSON.stringify(...)` upstream (e.g. snapshot-picks, check-pull-stats). There is no isFinite/replacer guard anywhere in this module.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: The screener computes ratios (ROIC, R40, growth rates) where a divide-by-zero or missing-denominator yields NaN/Infinity. If such a value reaches writeJsonAtomic, it is silently persisted as `null` — indistinguishable downstream from 'genuinely absent'. A reader then treats a computation error as missing data (often defaulting via `|| 0`), so a broken metric masquerades as a benign gap. This is the silent NaN-propagation / data-integrity class: the atomic-write hardening guarantees the bytes are durable but not that they are *meaningful*. Because this is the designated single-source-of-truth writer, a guard here protects every caller at once.
nonScoring.fix: Add an optional finite-number assertion path: accept `opts.assertFinite` (default off to preserve behaviour) that runs a replacer rejecting NaN/Infinity by throwing, so a corrupt computation fails loudly at write time instead of persisting `null`. Comment: '// prevents NaN/Infinity from a broken ratio being silently persisted as null and later read back as benign-missing'. Do not change the default for non-opted callers to avoid breaking existing writes; wire fitness/measure.js and score-output writers to pass assertFinite:true.

nonScoring.title: Synchronous busy/Atomics.wait sleep inside the Windows rename-retry loop blocks the event loop for up to 380ms per contended write during the pull
nonScoring.evidence: _sleepSync (line 70) uses `Atomics.wait` (or a `while (Date.now() < end)` busy-spin fallback) and is called from _renameWithRetry (line 93) for each of RENAME_RETRY_DELAYS_MS = [10,20,50,100,200] (sum 380ms) on Windows EPERM/EBUSY/EACCES. pull-yahoo.js writes one snapshot per ticker through writeFileAtomic (lines 1664, 2156, 2216, 2284, etc.) across the whole universe.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: On Karl's Windows box, OneDrive sync + AV scanners are exactly the handle-holders this retry was built for (the module comment says so). During the multi-hour pull, every contended rename can block the single thread for up to 380ms synchronously — and because writeFileAtomic is intentionally sync, this stalls the async Yahoo fetch pipeline too, not just the write. Across a large universe with frequent OneDrive contention this is a real, if modest, contributor to the 14.6h pull wall-clock. Low severity because correctness is preserved and the per-file cost is bounded.
nonScoring.fix: Keep the sync contract (callers rely on it) but consider: (a) writing snapshots to a non-OneDrive-synced temp/staging dir and moving in bulk after the pull, removing the dominant contention source; or (b) trimming the retry ladder on Windows (the [100,200] tail rarely helps for sub-50ms transient locks). If neither, document the worst-case stall. Do not convert to async (would force a large caller refactor against the module's stated design).

nonScoring.title: Keyed-map heuristic uses a strict majority test that can still misread a small mixed object, and silently yields shape 'object' with a synthetic ticker array
nonScoring.evidence: Line 63: `const looksKeyedMap = keys.length > 0 && tickerLike.length * 2 > keys.length;` then line 65 returns `{ shape: 'object', stocks: keys.map(...) }`. For a tiny object like `{ AAPL: {...}, note: 'x' }` (2 keys, 1 ticker-like since 'note' is a string not object) -> tickerLike=1, 1*2=2 > 2 is false -> invalid (good). But `{ AAPL: {...}, MSFT: {...}, _meta: 'x' }` -> tickerLike=2, 2*2=4 > 3 true -> treated as keyed map, and `_meta` (string) is mapped to `{ ticker:'_meta', 0:'x'... }` via Object.assign of a string, injecting a junk synthetic stock.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: The synthetic-array branch will faithfully convert EVERY key including non-ticker metadata keys once the majority test passes, because the map step (line 65) does not re-apply the TICKER_KEY_RE / typeof-object filter used to *detect* the shape. A stray metadata key on a legacy keyed-map watchlist becomes a phantom stock with a garbage ticker, which then flows into universeSize / drift-gate counts in check-pull-stats.js — subtly inflating the universe count the drift gate compares against. The keyed-map shape is 'long-retired' per the docstring, so exposure is low, but the asymmetry (detect with a filter, map without one) is a latent correctness gap.
nonScoring.fix: When building the synthetic array, reuse the same predicate: `keys.filter(k => TICKER_KEY_RE.test(k) && raw[k] && typeof raw[k]==='object').map(k => Object.assign({ticker:k}, raw[k]))`. This guarantees the emitted stocks are exactly the ticker-like, object-valued keys that justified the 'object' classification — comment: '// prevents metadata keys on a legacy keyed-map from becoming phantom stocks that inflate the drift-gate universe count'.

nonScoring.title: 13F tests mutate the REAL production cache (external-data/sec-13f-by-ticker.json) and run in CI — a crash/timeout in the stub→restore window leaves the 85KB production cache as a 1-entry stub
nonScoring.evidence: const CACHE_PATH_13F = path.join(__dirname, 'external-data', 'sec-13f-by-ticker.json'); ... function _stubCache(obj){ _writeCacheRaw(JSON.stringify(obj)); inst13fModule._resetCacheForTests(); } and in each test: const orig=_readCacheRaw(); try{ _stubCache({...byTicker:{TESTCO:...}}); ... } finally { _restoreCache(orig); }. The path is the live cache: `ls external-data` shows sec-13f-by-ticker.json = 85173 bytes, present in the worktree. daily-pull.yml:88 runs `node tag28-tests.js` in that same worktree, and method-types.js:100 marks institutional-ownership-13f defaultActive:true, so the very next pipeline step reads this file.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: The comment at line 1852-1857 claims routing the write through writeFileAtomic 'prevents non-atomic-write-truncates-production-cache'. That is a misdiagnosis: writeFileAtomic only makes a SINGLE write atomic. The real hazard is the test deliberately OVERWRITING production data with a 1-ticker stub and relying on a finally-block restore. If the Node process is SIGKILLed / hits the CI job timeout / OOMs while the stub is on disk (between _stubCache and _restoreCache), the 85KB smart-money cache is permanently replaced by {byTicker:{TESTCO:...}}. Every subsequent screener run then sees institutional-ownership-13f as not-computable for the entire universe (silent signal loss across ~all tickers) until the next 13F pull regenerates it — and daily-pull.yml has no 13F-regen step after the test. This is exactly the 'silently swallowed / non-atomic state' class the audit targets, made worse because it is self-inflicted by the test suite.
nonScoring.fix: Do NOT touch the real cache path from tests. Inject the cache location instead of hardcoding it: give institutional-ownership-13f a setter (e.g. _setCachePathForTests) or have _evaluateWithCache(stock, cacheObj) like ICS._evaluateWithTxns / momModule already do. Point the tests at a path under os.tmpdir()/a tests/-local fixture file, or pass the stub object directly. This removes all production-file I/O from the suite and makes the writeFileAtomic plumbing unnecessary.

nonScoring.title: _restoreCache(null) / _writeCacheRaw(null) call fs.unlinkSync on the real production cache — if the cache is momentarily absent at test start, the real file gets DELETED
nonScoring.evidence: function _writeCacheRaw(s){ if (s == null){ try{ fs.unlinkSync(CACHE_PATH_13F); }catch(e){} return; } ... }  function _restoreCache(originalRaw){ if (originalRaw == null){ try{ fs.unlinkSync(CACHE_PATH_13F); }catch(e){} } else _writeCacheRaw(originalRaw); ... }. orig comes from _readCacheRaw() which returns null on ANY read error (catch(e){return null;}), not only 'file absent'.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: _readCacheRaw swallows every error to null (transient EBUSY/locked file on Windows, a concurrent writer, a permissions blip). When orig===null for a transient reason, the test still stubs the cache, then 'restores' by UNLINKING the real 85KB production file. The deletion is also silently swallowed (catch(e){}). Combined with finding 01 this turns a flaky read into permanent data loss of a production artifact, with zero log output. unlinkSync on shared production state from a unit test is unjustifiable.
nonScoring.fix: Eliminate per finding 01 (use a tmp/injected path so deleting it is harmless). If a real-path round-trip must stay, distinguish 'file genuinely absent' (fs.existsSync false) from 'read failed' and refuse to unlink on read-error; never unlink a production path from a test.

nonScoring.title: Fixture-hash golden test self-heals a missing tests/fixture-hash.txt by writing it and returning PASS — a deleted/absent golden file silently disarms the score-aggregator regression guard in CI
nonScoring.evidence: if (!fs.existsSync(FIXTURE_HASH_PATH)) { ... fs.writeFileSync(FIXTURE_HASH_PATH, computed + '\n'); console.log('  no prior fixture-hash — wrote initial ' + computed); return; }  — the test returns (counts as passed) instead of failing when the golden file is missing.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: This is the suite's only guard against silent behavior changes in score-aggregator (the whole 'fixture-hash invariant' the file repeatedly cites). tests/ is freshly created in this worktree (Jun 21 14:45) and tests/fixture-hash.txt is git-ignored / not guaranteed present on a clean CI checkout. On any runner where the file is absent, the golden test writes whatever the CURRENT code produces and reports PASS — so a real scoring regression introduced in the same commit is baselined as 'correct' and ships. A golden test that auto-adopts the observed output on a fresh checkout provides no protection exactly when you most need it. (The ALLOW_FIXTURE_CHANGE=1 path at 2803 is the intended escape hatch; the silent no-env path at 2809 should not exist.)
nonScoring.fix: On a missing golden file in normal (no-env) mode, FAIL with a clear message instructing the operator to run with ALLOW_FIXTURE_CHANGE=1 once to seed it. Commit tests/fixture-hash.txt to the repo (remove from .gitignore) so CI always has a real baseline to diff against.

nonScoring.title: Tests mutate shared module-level caches but reset without try/finally — a thrown assertion leaks stub state into later tests, making results order-dependent (false pass or false fail)
nonScoring.evidence: The hand-rolled harness: function test(name,fn){ try{ fn(); ... } catch(e){ ... } }. price-momentum tests call momModule._resetCacheForTests() at the START only (line 1962/1975/1986) with no finally; the fixture-hash test uses Helpers._setMediansForTest then restores in a finally (2774/2795 — correct), but the 13F tests' inst13fModule._resetCacheForTests() inside _stubCache/_restoreCache runs only if those helpers are reached. There is no global afterEach reset.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: momModule and inst13fModule hold a process-global _cache. If an assertion throws between a reset and the next reset (e.g. price-momentum PASS test fails on barsUsed), the cache populated from the failing test's stub persists into the next test, which can then read stale data and either spuriously pass (masking a real defect) or spuriously fail (false alarm). Reset-at-start-without-finally is fragile: the suite's correctness depends on every test fully completing. This is the classic shared-mutable-state test-isolation bug; it also makes the fixture-hash determinism the suite advertises unreliable if a medians/cache reset is skipped.
nonScoring.fix: Reset all injectable caches in a finally per test (or add an afterEach hook to the harness that calls each module's _resetCacheForTests). Better: stop relying on module-global caches in tests — pass state explicitly via the _evaluateWith* injection seams that already exist for ICS.

nonScoring.title: Harness cannot detect async failures or hangs: test() only catches synchronous throws, and exit code is derived solely from a sync `failed` counter with no per-test timeout
nonScoring.evidence: function test(name, fn){ try{ fn(); console.log(' V '+name); passed++; } catch(e){ ... failed++; } }  ... process.exit(failed > 0 ? 1 : 0);  — fn is invoked synchronously; a returned Promise rejection would be unobserved, and an infinite loop in any method has no timeout.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: All current tests are synchronous, but the suite tests the data pipeline whose modules increasingly touch fs and could become async. Any future async method (or an accidentally-async assertion) would always report PASS because the rejection lands after process.exit. And because tag28-tests.js is a CI pre-pull GUARD (daily-pull.yml:88, 'Schützt gegen production-Schäden'), a hang means the daily pull stalls with no signal rather than failing fast. A guard you trust to protect production should fail closed on async errors and on timeout.
nonScoring.fix: Detect Promise returns from fn and await/flag them; install a process-level unhandledRejection handler that bumps `failed`; wrap the whole run with a watchdog timer (or migrate to node:test / a real runner that handles async + timeouts natively).

nonScoring.title: FX conversion test asserts a hardcoded USD range tied to mutable live fx-rates.json — couples a 'unit' test to external market data and will false-fail CI when TWD moves outside 0.020–0.050
nonScoring.evidence: PY._convertSnapshotToUSD(twdSnap); ... if (twdSnap.marketCap.value > 50e9 || twdSnap.marketCap.value < 10e9) { throw new Error('TWD mcap outside expected USD range...'); }  with comment 'TWD rate ~0.030–0.033'. The same module loads the real fx-rates.json (present, Jun 20).
nonScoring.why_it_matters: The test author already half-acknowledges the coupling (lines 421-424 deliberately avoid checking absolute USD values 'because the live FX rate ... may differ'), yet still hardcodes a 10e9–50e9 absolute USD window. 1000B TWD at the asserted band implies a rate of 0.010–0.050; a sustained TWD revaluation or a stale/bad fx-rates.json entry pushes the converted mcap out of band and red-fails the CI pre-pull guard for a reason unrelated to code correctness — and because this guard gates the daily pull, a bad FX feed would block the whole pipeline. It also means the test can PASS while the FX file is silently wrong, as long as the product stays in [10e9,50e9].
nonScoring.fix: Stub the FX rate the same way ICS stubs Date.now()/txns: inject a fixed fx map into _convertSnapshotToUSD (or read the rate the test expects and assert mcap == 1000e9 * thatRate within tolerance). Assert only currency-INVARIANT properties (the FCF-yield and rev/mcap ratio checks at 445-453 are correct and sufficient); drop the absolute USD-range assertion.

nonScoring.title: 2825-line god test-file with a hand-rolled runner conflates ~50 module unit tests, a CI fixture-hash golden, and live production-file I/O in one process
nonScoring.evidence: Single file, 155971 bytes, one shared `passed/failed` counter, ~250 inline test() calls spanning rule-of-40 through Buffett-criteria, plus _computeFixtureHash (2763) and real-cache I/O (1859). No test runner; assertions are ad-hoc throws.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: Everything shares one process and one global state, which is the root enabler of findings 01/02/04: a production-file mutation, a global-cache leak, and a golden-hash check all run in the same Node invocation with no isolation between them. It also caps maintainability — adding a method means editing a 2825-line file, and a single early throw/exit can skip the fixture-hash golden entirely (it is the LAST test, line 2799, so any earlier process.exit or crash silently skips the one check that guards scoring). This structurally limits the screener's test reliability, not just tidiness.
nonScoring.fix: Split into per-concern suites (methods unit tests; pipeline/pull-yahoo currency tests; the fixture-hash golden as its own file that runs FIRST or in its own job) and adopt node:test (built into Node >=22, already required per package.json engines) for isolation, async support, and timeouts. Run the fixture-hash golden as a dedicated CI step so it can never be skipped by an unrelated earlier failure.

nonScoring.title: data-quality grade tests over-fit exact nanRatio bookkeeping and magic weight arithmetic in comments, so a legitimate CRITICAL_FIELDS change forces brittle multi-test edits
nonScoring.evidence: if (g.nanRatio !== 0) throw ... and the ~30%-missing test hardcodes the derivation in a comment: 'total weight = 19.5. Drop 5 weight-1.0 fields (5/19.5 = 0.256) AND 4 weight-0.5 fields (2/19.5 = 0.103) for 0.359 total → A grade'. The boundaries (A ≤0.40, C ≤0.85) are pinned by exact field deletions.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: These assertions are tightly coupled to the internal weight table in data-quality.js. Any future addition/removal of a CRITICAL_FIELD (the file shows this has already happened repeatedly: Tag 211l/219/220c/232c-4) silently shifts nanRatio and flips the grade boundary, breaking the test for a non-bug reason and tempting a hand-tweak of the fixture rather than a real check. The test asserts implementation arithmetic, not the behavioral contract (grade buckets).
nonScoring.fix: Assert the behavioral boundary, not the exact ratio: drive nanRatio to just-below and just-above each threshold programmatically (compute from gradeSnapshot's own field list) and assert the resulting grade, so the test survives weight-table edits. Keep one explicit boundary test per grade transition rather than encoding the weight math in comments.

nonScoring.title: Two price pullers write DIFFERENT price semantics (raw close vs adjusted close) under the same `close` key into the same prices/history.json
nonScoring.evidence: pull-historical-prices.js:100-103 `const quotes = (result.quotes||[]).filter(q => (q.adjclose ?? q.close) != null); ... const latestClose = latestQuote.adjclose ?? latestQuote.close;` then :127 `arr.push({ date: latestQuoteDate, close: latestClose });` — stores ADJUSTED close under key `close`. pull-prices-bulk.js:56-59 `const quotes = (r.quotes||[]).filter(q => q.close != null).map(q => ({ date: ..., close: q.close }));` — stores RAW close under the same key. Both target the SAME file: pull-historical-prices histPath = path.join(args.out,'history.json') (:67,198); pull-prices-bulk HISTORY_PATH='./prices/history.json' (:10) merged via _safeMergeAndWrite (:37). The consumer walk-forward-perf.js:106 `new Map(entries.map(e => [e.date, e.close]))` and :147 `return chosen.close` reads `close` blindly with no idea which semantics produced it.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: Adjusted close back-applies every later split/dividend to ALL earlier dates, so an adjclose series and a raw-close series for the same ticker are on different scales. _safeMergeAndWrite does Object.assign(onDisk, myUpdates) (:36) → last-writer-wins per ticker, so a ticker's series silently flips between raw and adjusted depending on which script touched it last. walk-forward-perf computes returnPct(p0,p1)=(p1-p0)/p0 (:150-152) across dates; mixing scales (or a split landing between the two pull tools' runs) yields phantom returns of tens of percent. This directly corrupts the backtest/alpha numbers that are the screener's evidence base — a top contributor to it being 'at 20% of potential'.
nonScoring.fix: Make the two writers agree. Since pull-historical-prices.js is the workflow entrypoint and already standardized on adjclose (Tag 148), either (a) change pull-prices-bulk.js:58 to `close: (q.adjclose ?? q.close)`, or (b) store both fields and have priceAt read a named field. Prefer (a) plus renaming the stored field to `adjclose` everywhere so the semantics are self-documenting. Add a one-time migration note; do NOT mix. Tag the change with the failure mode it prevents.

nonScoring.line: 1-83 (whole file); confirmed absent from .github/workflows and from any require() in src
nonScoring.title: pull-prices-bulk.js is an orphan entrypoint that no workflow/script invokes yet still writes the shared history.json — a live foot-gun
nonScoring.evidence: grep for `pull-prices-bulk|prices-bulk` across .github returned 'No matches found'; no source .js require()s it (only findings/audit-reports JSON mention it). It is not in package.json scripts (only pull/pull:fast/pull:single → pull-yahoo.js). It exports `{ main, _safeMergeAndWrite }` and self-runs only under require.main (:78). It pulls 25 tickers per manual `node pull-prices-bulk.js <startIdx>` invocation (:46-47) and writes prices/history.json (:37).
nonScoring.why_it_matters: It is reachable only by a human typing the command, but when run it injects raw-close data into the same file the automated adjclose pipeline owns (see A-01), and its 100-day window (:53 `Date.now()-100*86400*1000`) vs pull-historical-prices' 400-day window (:94) means a manual backfill also truncates/disagrees on series length. Dead-but-armed code that mutates production state is worse than dead code: it invites the exact corruption A-01 describes. Either retire it or make it a thin, clearly-labeled backfill that shares the canonical writer.
nonScoring.fix: Decide its fate explicitly. If still wanted as a manual backfill, make it import the same write path AND adjclose semantics as pull-historical-prices.js (dedupe the _safeMergeAndWrite logic into lib/). If not, delete it (ask Karl before deleting per house rule). Do not leave a second writer with divergent semantics on a shared file.

nonScoring.title: Per-ticker history only ever appends the single latest trading day per run; new tickers get a 1-point series and no script back-fills them — walk-forward has near-zero history for most of the universe
nonScoring.evidence: processOne pulls 400 days (:94 period1) but then only keeps the LAST quote: :102 `const latestQuote = quotes[quotes.length-1];` :126-128 `if (arr.length===0 || arr[arr.length-1].date !== latestQuoteDate) arr.push({date: latestQuoteDate, close: latestClose});` — exactly one entry appended per run. Only SPY gets the full back-fill loop (:172-182 iterates ALL spyQuotes into history). A freshly-discovered ticker therefore has history length 1 after its first pull and grows by 1/day. The 400 days of data fetched over the wire are discarded for every non-SPY ticker.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: walk-forward-perf needs 84+ day vintages (daily-pull.yml:552) and priceAt walks back PRICE_MAX_STALE_DAYS=7 (walk-forward-perf.js:124) — a ticker added <90 trading days ago simply returns null for its entry price, silently excluding it from forward-return stats. Because refresh-universe adds new tickers constantly, a large rolling fraction of the universe is permanently un-backtestable. The pipeline pays full Yahoo bandwidth for 400-day pulls and throws 399/400 of it away. This is both a perf waste and the structural cap on backtest coverage.
nonScoring.fix: In processOne, back-fill the same way SPY is handled: build a Set of known dates for the ticker and insert every fetched quote that isn't present (mirror lines 172-180), then sort+trim to 400. One-time it fills history for the whole universe; steady-state it's a no-op append. Comment it with the failure mode (under-length series → null forward-return → survivorship-like exclusion).

nonScoring.title: QQQ and IWM benchmarks are injected but never back-filled — only SPY gets a full series, so alpha-vs-QQQ/IWM is computed on a 1-point benchmark
nonScoring.evidence: BENCHMARKS lists SPY, QQQ, IWM (:52-56) and unshifts all three into wl.stocks (:57-58). The dedicated full back-fill block (:150-191) is hardcoded to SPY only: `if (!history['SPY'] || !todaysSnapshot['SPY'])` and `yf.chart('SPY', ...)`. QQQ/IWM flow through the normal processOne path which (per A-03) appends only one point per run.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: The benchmark comment (:50-51) says the ETFs are pulled 'so walk-forward-perf can compute alpha vs SPY' — but the code only guarantees SPY a usable multi-year series. Any alpha/relative-strength computation against QQQ or IWM operates on a near-empty benchmark series and silently degrades to null or to a misleading value. Asymmetric benchmark coverage biases mode comparisons.
nonScoring.fix: Generalize the SPY back-fill block to loop over the BENCHMARKS array (and ideally all tickers per A-03). Keep the 'always ensure present' guard per benchmark. Comment with the failure mode (single-point benchmark → invalid alpha).

nonScoring.title: Corrupt existing aktienfinder.json is swallowed to `existing={}`, then the merge overwrites the recoverable file with ONLY the new CSV — silent total history loss
nonScoring.evidence: Lines 34-37: `let existing = {}; if (fs.existsSync(outPath)) { try { existing = JSON.parse(...); } catch (e) { console.warn('Failed to load aktienfinder.json:', e.message); } }` then :38 `const merged = Object.assign(existing, data);` and :39 `writeFileAtomic(outPath, JSON.stringify(merged,null,2));`. On a parse failure `existing` stays `{}`, so `merged` is just the current CSV and the atomic write durably replaces the previously-good (now corrupt-but-recoverable) file with a stripped-down version.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: This is the exact F-SM-015 / F-SC-028 pattern the team already fixed in pull-historical-prices.js (:62-82 back up + refuse) and pull-prices-bulk.js (:27-34 _backupCorrupt) — aktienfinder-import was missed. A single truncated write (Ctrl-C, OneDrive sync race, disk full) on a manual import permanently discards every previously-imported Aktienfinder score, which feeds the scoring layer. writeFileAtomic makes the destructive overwrite durable, ironically guaranteeing the loss.
nonScoring.fix: On JSON.parse failure: back up the corrupt file (rename to outPath + '.corrupt.' + Date.now()) and either abort unless an explicit RESET env is set, or at minimum refuse to write a merge whose base was lost. Reuse the established pull-historical-prices.js pattern. Add the failure-mode comment.

nonScoring.title: Earnings date derived by truncating a UTC ISO string — off-by-one day for any earnings timestamp in evening US time, shifting the calendar date downstream
nonScoring.evidence: Line 33: `const iso = (first instanceof Date) ? first.toISOString() : (first && first.raw ? new Date(first.raw*1000).toISOString() : null);` :34 `result[stock.ticker] = { date: iso.slice(0,10), ... }`. `toISOString()` is UTC; `.slice(0,10)` takes the UTC calendar date. Yahoo earningsDate timestamps are commonly set to a local exchange date that, expressed in UTC, can roll into the next or previous day.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: The consumer earnings-cli.js:42 does `new Date(info.date)` (parses 'YYYY-MM-DD' as UTC midnight) and compares `d >= today` where today is LOCAL midnight (:36 `today.setHours(0,0,0,0)`). A UTC-shifted date plus the local/UTC comparison mismatch can drop an earnings event from the 'next N days' window or list it on the wrong day, so an earnings-proximity filter or alert misfires by a day. For an earnings-sensitive screener that's a real signal error.
nonScoring.fix: Either keep the full timestamp and let the consumer do timezone-aware comparison, or derive the date in the exchange's local zone. At minimum, make pull and consumer agree on UTC: in earnings-cli compare against a UTC `today` (Date.UTC(...)) rather than local. Comment the boundary failure mode on the method side.

nonScoring.title: startIdx/endIdx parsed with no NaN/bounds guard — a non-numeric or out-of-range arg yields a silent zero-iteration no-op reported as success
nonScoring.evidence: Line 46: `const startIdx = parseInt(process.argv[2] || '0', 10);` :47 `const endIdx = Math.min(startIdx+25, wl.stocks.length);`. `parseInt('abc',10)` → NaN; then `NaN+25`=NaN, `Math.min(NaN, len)`=NaN; the loop `for (let i=startIdx; i<endIdx; ...)` (:49) compares NaN<NaN = false → zero iterations. The console prints `Processing stocks NaN..NaN of N` (:48) and `Done range NaN-NaN` (:70), exit 0.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: A typo or a shell-variable that didn't expand silently pulls nothing, writes nothing, and exits clean — a batch orchestration looping over ranges would 'succeed' while skipping chunks, leaving holes in history with no error. Combined with continue-on-error workflows this is exactly the silent-success failure class the audit targets.
nonScoring.fix: Validate: `if (!Number.isFinite(startIdx) || startIdx < 0 || startIdx >= wl.stocks.length) { console.error('startIdx out of range'); process.exit(1); }`. Mirror earnings-cli.js:18-21's existing guard pattern.

nonScoring.title: main() invoked without .catch and without require.main guard — a watchlist parse error becomes an unhandled rejection (exit 0 in older Node / silent) and require()ing the file auto-runs a live Yahoo pull
nonScoring.evidence: Line 50 is bare `main();`. There is no `.catch(e => { ...; process.exit(1); })` and no `if (require.main === module)` guard. Contrast the sibling scripts which already adopted both: pull-prices-bulk.js:78-82 and pull-sec-xbrl.js:206-208 do `if (require.main === module) main().catch(e => { console.error(e); process.exit(1); });` and `module.exports`.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: (1) Silent failure: the workflow step runs with continue-on-error (daily-pull.yml:468); an unhandled rejection that exits 0 lets CI treat a totally failed earnings pull as success — earnings-calendar.json stays stale and no one is alerted. (2) Auto-run-on-require: if any test or aggregator ever `require`s this file it immediately fires a real Yahoo quoteSummary storm over the whole watchlist. This is the same defect already fixed in pull-prices-bulk.js (its own comment block :73-77 documents exactly this).
nonScoring.fix: Wrap as `if (require.main === module) { main().catch(e => { console.error('pull-earnings-dates failed:', e.stack||e.message); process.exit(1); }); } module.exports = { main };` — copy the pattern from pull-prices-bulk.js / pull-sec-xbrl.js verbatim.

nonScoring.title: Between-batch sleep is a fixed 300ms that ignores how long the batch's own Promise.all took — rate-limit pacing is the tail latency, not the gap
nonScoring.evidence: Lines 39-45: `for (... batchStart += CONCURRENCY) { const batch = wl.stocks.slice(...); await Promise.all(batch.map(s => processOne(s).catch(()=>{}))); if (batchStart + CONCURRENCY < wl.stocks.length) await sleep(300); }`. The 300ms is added AFTER awaiting the whole batch, so when a batch returns fast (cache hits / fast network) 15 concurrent quoteSummary calls fire, then only 300ms passes before the next 15 — bursts of 15 every ~300ms+batchtime.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: Earnings pulls hit the same Yahoo Cloudflare edge that forced PULL_CONCURRENCY and EARNINGS_CONCURRENCY down to 8 (daily-pull.yml:42,465 — the Tag 215f lesson). A fixed post-batch gap with concurrency 15 (default :24) or even 8 can still micro-burst and trigger 429s, which are then swallowed by the per-item empty catch (:36) so the calendar silently under-populates. Lower-severity because errors are tolerated, but it caps reliable coverage.
nonScoring.fix: Either lower default EARNINGS_CONCURRENCY to match the workflow's 8, or pace by elapsed time: record batch start, sleep `max(0, minInterval - elapsed)`. Add the rate-limit-boundary failure-mode comment.

nonScoring.title: Periodic manifest flush keyed on (pulled+skipped304)%100 — runs dominated by 404/error/304 can complete with zero intermediate persistence, and a mid-run abort loses all manifest progress
nonScoring.evidence: Line 192: `if ((pulled + skipped304) % 100 === 0 && (pulled + skipped304) > 0) { ... writeFileAtomic(MANIFEST_PATH, ...); }`. The counter excludes notFound, errors, rateLimited and skippedFresh. On a corpus where most CIKs are 404 (delisted) or fresh-skip, `pulled+skipped304` may crawl; if the run is SIGKILLed (CI timeout) before it crosses a multiple of 100, the manifest written this run is only the final write at :202 — never reached on abort.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: The manifest is the resume cursor (fetchedAt drives the staleness skip at :145 and the --max least-recently-fetched sort at :132-138). Losing a run's manifest progress means the next run re-pulls everything it already fetched, wasting the SEC rate budget and never advancing through a ~10k-CIK corpus that --max can only chip at. The notFound markers (:156) that prevent re-hitting dead CIKs are also lost on abort. The whole point of the periodic flush — surviving the abort the comment at :194 cites — is defeated for error/404-heavy runs.
nonScoring.fix: Flush on total processed (pulled+skipped304+notFound+errors+rateLimited) % 100, or simpler: flush every N iterations of the loop regardless of outcome, and/or install a SIGTERM/SIGINT handler that writes the manifest before exit. Comment the failure mode (lost resume cursor → re-pull storm).

nonScoring.title: Watchlist merge assumes every existing and discovered stock has a defined `ticker` — a single null/undefined ticker throws on .toUpperCase()/.localeCompare and aborts the whole universe refresh
nonScoring.evidence: Line 205: `const existing = new Set(wlRaw.stocks.map(s => s.ticker.toUpperCase()));` — no guard; any stock with a missing/null `ticker` throws TypeError. Line 449: `wlRaw.stocks.sort((a,b) => a.ticker.localeCompare(b.ticker));` — same exposure after merge. The new-ticker objects are built from discovery sources (:438-447) using `info.ticker`; if any source ever yields an entry without ticker the sort throws.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: refresh-universe runs first in the daily workflow (daily-pull.yml:112-122). Although that step is continue-on-error, a throw here means the universe is never refreshed — new IPOs/mid-caps stop entering, and over time the universe stagnates (the asymmetric-attrition / survivorship concern), while the failure is masked by continue-on-error and only the downstream 'size < 200' floor (:148) would catch a catastrophic case, not a no-op. One malformed discovery row silently freezes universe growth.
nonScoring.fix: Guard the maps: `wlRaw.stocks.map(s => s.ticker).filter(Boolean).map(t => t.toUpperCase())` for the Set, skip ticker-less entries when building newTickers, and make the sort null-safe (`(a.ticker||'').localeCompare(b.ticker||'')`). Comment the failure mode (one bad row → frozen universe).

nonScoring.title: marketCap kept via `(allTickers.get(sym).marketCap || 0) < mcap` and capped via `b[1].marketCap - a[1].marketCap` — non-finite/NaN marketCap from a source poisons the dedupe and the rank-sort
nonScoring.evidence: Line 232/286: `if (!allTickers.has(sym) || (allTickers.get(sym).marketCap || 0) < mcap)` — `mcap` itself passed the `!mcap||mcap<1e9||mcap>500e9` guard (:231/285) so it's finite here, OK; but the STORED side uses `|| 0`, and a later discovery-source merge can set `marketCap: info.marketCap || null` (:345). At cap time :390 `withMcap.sort((a,b) => b[1].marketCap - a[1].marketCap)` after filtering `v.marketCap != null && v.marketCap > 0` (:386) — that filter screens null but NOT NaN (NaN != null is true, NaN > 0 is false, so NaN rows actually fall into withoutMcap — acceptable), however any Infinity from a bad source would sort to the top and crowd out real names.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: Lower severity because the explicit range guard on the screener path blocks most junk, but the discovery-source merge path (:340-350) trusts `info.marketCap` unchecked. A source emitting Infinity/huge bogus mcap would rank-sort to the front of withMcap and consume top slots under the MAX_UNIVERSE cap, displacing legitimate large caps — a silent universe-composition bias.
nonScoring.fix: Normalize on ingest: when storing marketCap, coerce with `Number.isFinite(m) && m>0 ? m : null`. Then the existing null-bucket logic handles it correctly. One-line guard at each `allTickers.set`.

nonScoring.title: BENCHMARKS are unshift-ed into the in-memory watchlist every run but the watchlist is read-only here — harmless now, but couples benchmark identity to ticker-string equality and will silently double-insert if yahoo_symbol ever differs from ticker
nonScoring.evidence: Lines 57-58: `for (const b of BENCHMARKS) { if (!wl.stocks.find(s => s.ticker === b.ticker)) wl.stocks.unshift(b); }`. The dedupe is by `s.ticker === b.ticker` exact case-sensitive match. wl is not written back (good), but processOne keys snapshots/history by `stock.ticker` (:116,119) — if the real watchlist already contains 'SPY' with a different yahoo_symbol or lower-case variant, the find misses and a duplicate benchmark row is processed.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: Minor today (watchlist tickers are uppercase), but it's a latent off-by-identity bug: the .find uses ticker while the rest of the system has both `ticker` and `yahoo_symbol` fields that can diverge (refresh-universe sets yahoo_symbol = ticker at :441 but external sources need not). A duplicate SPY would get processed twice and the second pass is a redundant Yahoo call.
nonScoring.fix: Dedupe case-insensitively and consider yahoo_symbol: `if (!wl.stocks.some(s => (s.ticker||'').toUpperCase() === b.ticker))`. Low priority; bundle with A-03/A-04 benchmark cleanup.

nonScoring.title: todaysSnapshot keyed close uses adjclose but the per-day prices/<date>.json `asOf` is calendar `today`, not the actual trading date — re-introduces the weekend phantom-date the history fix (Tag 231a-3) deliberately removed
nonScoring.evidence: Line 116: `todaysSnapshot[stock.ticker] = { close: latestClose, asOf: today, currency: ... };` where `today = new Date().toISOString().slice(0,10)` (:60). The history array was specifically fixed to use `latestQuoteDate` (the real exchange date, :113-114,127) to avoid mapping Saturday→Friday's price, but the per-day snapshot file still stamps `asOf: today`. On a weekend/holiday run, prices/2026-06-21.json (Sat) contains Friday's adjclose labeled asOf Saturday.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: Any consumer that trusts the per-day file's asOf (rather than history's dated entries) gets the same phantom-date inconsistency the team already paid to eliminate in history.json. It's lower severity because walk-forward reads history.json (dated correctly) not the per-day files, but check-pull-stats and other readers of prices/<date>.json may mis-date the latest close, and it's an avoidable internal inconsistency between the two outputs of the same function.
nonScoring.fix: Set `asOf: latestQuoteDate` in todaysSnapshot to match the history entry, or store both `asOf: today` (run date) and `tradeDate: latestQuoteDate` explicitly. Comment with the weekend-phantom-date failure mode (cross-reference Tag 231a-3).

nonScoring.title: blockedByOneMust ignores 'incomputable' MUSTs — Near-Miss panel mislabels multi-barrier stocks as one-barrier
nonScoring.evidence: Line 190-192: `if (!me || me.passed || !me.mustResults) continue; const failed = me.mustResults.filter(m => m.status === 'fail'); if (failed.length !== 1) continue;`. In strategy-modes.js a MUST can resolve to three states: 'pass', 'fail', or 'incomputable' (line 234: `mustResults.push({ id: check.id, status: 'incomputable', ... })`). `allMustPass` requires mustPassCount===mustChecks.length, so an incomputable MUST also blocks passing. blockedByOneMust only counts status==='fail'.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: A stock with exactly 1 failing MUST but 2 incomputable MUSTs (missing data) is presented to Karl under 'Scheitert an: <oneMust>' as if a single threshold tweak would unlock it. It actually has 3 barriers. This is the exact 'which compounders fail at only one threshold' diagnostic the panel exists for (Tag 121b comment) — so the panel systematically overstates how close stocks are, polluting the Tag-122 threshold-tuning decision. Conversely a stock failing 1 + incomputable 1 is shown identically to a clean 1-fail near-miss.
nonScoring.fix: Treat incomputable as a blocking barrier: count both. e.g. `const blocking = me.mustResults.filter(m => m.status === 'fail' || m.status === 'incomputable'); if (blocking.length !== 1) continue;` then key the bucket on blocking[0]. If the intent is strictly 'one *threshold* miss', then additionally exclude any stock with incomputable MUSTs from the panel rather than silently ignoring them. Add a comment naming the failure mode (incomputable-MUST hidden as clean near-miss).

nonScoring.title: dedupeByCompany name-collision + unconditional US-preference silently drops distinct/larger foreign companies (survivorship asymmetry)
nonScoring.evidence: key = norm(name) collapses on a heavily stripped, accent-folded, suffix-stripped, alnum-only string (lines 202-223). On collision the tiebreak is `if (evIsUS && !exIsUS) keep = ev; else if (!evIsUS && exIsUS) keep = existing;` (lines 235-236) — US listing wins regardless of mcap or data completeness; only when both are same-nationality does mcap decide (line 237).
nonScoring.why_it_matters: Two genuinely different companies whose names normalize to the same token (short common stems after suffix/accent stripping) are merged, deleting one from every mode's universe — pure survivorship attrition that never surfaces in the health gate (dedupe drop count is logged only as a total on line 1314, not per-collision). The US-always-wins rule means a foreign large-cap primary listing can be evicted by a tiny US ADR/shadow of a *different* company sharing a normalized name. For a discovery screener aiming at international growth names, this asymmetrically thins the non-US set.
nonScoring.fix: Make the key collision-resistant: include a discriminator (e.g. first ~6 chars of normalized name + rounded log10(mcap) bucket, or require sector match before merging). For the cross-listing tiebreak, prefer the listing with more populated annual/timeseries data or higher mcap rather than nationality; only use US-preference as a final tiebreak when data and mcap are comparable. Log merged pairs (key, dropped ticker, kept ticker) so attrition is auditable.

nonScoring.title: IPO-year filter breaks when the universe contains stocks with ipoYear === 0/null (ipoMin slider can exclude every undated stock or none)
nonScoring.evidence: Server: `const ipos = eligible.map(e => e.ipoYear||0).filter(Boolean); const ipoMin = ipos.length ? Math.min(...ipos) : 1962;` (473-474). Card emits `data-ipo="${ipoYear||0}"` (line 436). Client: `ipoMin` slider default = server ipoMin (line 567), `ipoActive = ipoMin > ipoDefault` (line 1155), `ipoOk = !ipoActive || (ipo > 0 && ipo >= ipoMin)` (line 1176).
nonScoring.why_it_matters: Stocks with no ipoYear get data-ipo=0. As soon as Karl nudges the 'IPO seit' slider above the default minimum, ipoActive flips true and the `ipo > 0` clause hard-excludes every undated stock — even names that IPO'd long before the chosen year. The count 'sichtbar' silently drops a whole cohort of legitimate old companies purely because Yahoo lacked an IPO date. This is invisible (no 'undated' bucket), so Karl reads the filtered list as complete.
nonScoring.fix: Decide the undated policy explicitly and document it: either keep undated stocks visible whenever the IPO filter is active (treat missing ipo as 'unknown, do not exclude') or surface an 'IPO unbekannt' toggle. Concretely change the client predicate to `ipoOk = !ipoActive || ipo === 0 || ipo >= ipoMin` and label undated cards so the user knows they are unfiltered.

nonScoring.title: Country filter and modal use two different country sources (region-derived vs raw meta.country) — filter and detail disagree
nonScoring.evidence: Card data-country is region-derived: `const country = REGION_TO_COUNTRY[region] || region || '';` (line 376) and emitted as data-country (line 436); the sidebar country list is also built from REGION_TO_COUNTRY (line 471). But the modal/stockDataMap stores `country: (s.meta && s.meta.country) || ''` (line 382), shown in the modal header (line 1102). The client country filter compares data-country (region-derived) against the region-derived dropdown (line 1178).
nonScoring.why_it_matters: The detail panel can display a different country than the one the stock was filtered under (e.g. region 'NasdaqGS' → data-country 'USA' for filtering, while meta.country might be 'Israel' for an Israeli ADR). The filter therefore groups by *exchange region*, not domicile, which for ADRs and cross-listings misclassifies the company's actual country — undermining the 'Land' filter's purpose for an international screener and confusing Karl when the modal contradicts the filter bucket.
nonScoring.fix: Pick one country source of truth. Prefer meta.country (domicile) for both the filter dropdown, the card data-country, and the modal — falling back to REGION_TO_COUNTRY[region] only when meta.country is absent. Build the sidebar country options from the same resolved value used on the cards.

nonScoring.title: REJECT/untiered stocks are rendered into the Picks view but excluded from the Picks count — count understates what is shown
nonScoring.evidence: groups now includes a REJECT bucket and renderTierGroup('Reject — Score < 50 / untiered', groups.REJECT, 'reject') is appended to picksHtml (line 509). But picksTotal = `groups.A.length + groups.B.length + groups.NEAR_MISS.length + groups.RED_FLAG.length` (line 535) — REJECT omitted. picksTotal drives both the sidebar 'sichtbar' seed (line 578) and the 'Picks <count>' tab badge (line 585).
nonScoring.why_it_matters: The Picks panel visibly renders REJECT cards (the F-A-2026-06-21 fix deliberately stopped hiding them), yet the headline count and the live 'sichtbar' counter exclude them. On initial load the tab says e.g. 'Picks 40' while 60 cards are visible; applyFilters then recomputes a different number on first interaction, so the count jumps without the user touching anything. Erodes trust in the headline numbers.
nonScoring.fix: Either include groups.REJECT.length in picksTotal (if REJECT cards are meant to count as picks) or do not render the REJECT group inside the Picks panel (move it to its own collapsed section). Keep the rendered set and the count definitionally identical.

nonScoring.title: RED_FLAG bucket is effectively unreachable for A/B because the aggregator already downgrades red-flagged A/B to NEAR_MISS
nonScoring.evidence: renderModeContent buckets with RED_FLAG first: `if (me.redFlags && me.redFlags.length > 0) groups.RED_FLAG.push(ev);` (line 486). But score-aggregator.js line 413-414 already does `if (redFlags.length > 0 && (tier === 'A' || tier === 'B')) tier = 'NEAR_MISS';` — so by the time tier is read here, any red-flagged former-A/B carries tier NEAR_MISS, and a red-flagged NEAR_MISS/REJECT also has redFlags set. The RED_FLAG group therefore captures *all* red-flagged stocks regardless of underlying score, while the NEAR_MISS bucket only gets red-flag-free 50-64 stocks.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: Two layers (aggregator + report) both act on redFlags, so the report's tier groupings no longer mean what their headers say: a genuine score-78 name with one red flag lands under 'Red-Flag' next to a score-20 red-flagged reject, and the 'Near-Miss — Score 50-64' header excludes red-flagged 50-64 names. The grouping is driven by an implicit double-handling that will drift if either layer changes. Not a data-loss bug, but a correctness/clarity defect in how picks are presented.
nonScoring.fix: Decide ownership of the red-flag downgrade in exactly one place. If the report wants a dedicated Red-Flag section, gate it on score band too (e.g. only show red-flagged A/B-raw there) and let the aggregator stop mutating tier; or keep the aggregator's downgrade and drop the separate RED_FLAG bucket in favor of an inline red-flag badge. Document which layer owns it.

nonScoring.title: FCF/Growth filters silently pass any card whose metric is 'n/a' even when the user set a strict floor
nonScoring.evidence: `var fcfOk = (fcfMin <= -30) || card.dataset.fcfMargin === 'n/a' || (Number.isFinite(fcfM) && fcfM >= fcfMin);` (line 1179) and the symmetric `growthOk` (line 1180). When the metric is missing, data-fcf-margin is the string 'n/a' (set on line 436 when !Number.isFinite), so the second clause unconditionally keeps the card.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: If Karl drags 'FCF-Marge >= +20%' he expects only cards proven to clear +20%. Instead every card lacking an FCF figure stays visible, so the filtered list is contaminated with unknowns presented alongside qualifying names. For a quality/compounder workflow this defeats the filter's purpose and can put data-poor names in front of Karl as if they passed a profitability bar. The same applies to the growth floor.
nonScoring.fix: Make the missing-data policy explicit and probably exclusionary when a strict floor is set: `var fcfOk = (fcfMin <= -30) || (Number.isFinite(fcfM) && fcfM >= fcfMin);` (drop the n/a pass-through), or add a visible 'inkl. ohne Daten' checkbox. At minimum, style n/a cards distinctly so the user knows they were not actually tested against the floor.

nonScoring.title: Unguarded mode.enabled access assumes every key in SM.MODES resolves to a defined mode object
nonScoring.evidence: renderModeContent: `const mode = SM.MODES[modeId]; if (mode.enabled === false) {...}` (lines 462-463) dereferences mode without a null check. eligibleForMode does the same: `const mode = SM.MODES[modeId]; if (mode.enabled === false) return [];` (lines 254-255). buildHtml iterates `Object.keys(SM.MODES)` so today modeId always exists, but the modeLabels/modeMeta maps (lines 635-646) and topTabs hardcode HYPERGROWTH/QUALITY_COMPOUNDER/BUFFETT/TURNAROUND.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: The label/meta maps are maintained separately from SM.MODES. If a new mode key is added to strategy-modes.js, Object.keys picks it up and renders a tab with `undefined` label (modeLabels[m] → undefined, line 656) and meta, while any code path passing a stale/removed modeId would throw `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'enabled')` and kill the whole report via the top-level catch (line 1366). The coupling between the MODES registry and the three hardcoded presentation maps is fragile.
nonScoring.fix: Guard the dereference (`if (!mode || mode.enabled === false)`) and derive modeLabels/modeMeta defaults from the mode object (mode.label / mode.id) so a newly added mode renders sanely instead of `undefined` or crashing. Keep the presentation maps as overrides, not the sole source.

nonScoring.title: Mode-eval failure gate divides by stocks.length (post-load) not the effective universe, diluting a systemic mode break below threshold
nonScoring.evidence: The per-stock gate correctly uses the parse-error-inflated universe: `n_total = stocks.length + n_parse_errors` (line 1336). But the mode-eval gate uses `const mode_eval_total = stocks.length * Object.keys(SM.MODES).length;` (line 1353) — excluding parse-error files — and `mode_eval_rate = n_mode_eval_errors / mode_eval_total`.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: Inconsistent denominators between the two gates. More importantly, modeEvalErrors are only incremented for stocks that *survived* loading and the outer try (line 132); stocks killed by the outer per-stock catch (line 138-141) never enter the mode loop, so the numerator omits whole-stock failures while the denominator assumes every loaded stock ran every mode. A wave of stocks throwing in Runner.evaluateStock inflates _pipelineFailures (caught by gate 1) but artificially depresses mode_eval_rate, which could mask a *correlated* mode-level break that only manifests on the stocks that did evaluate.
nonScoring.fix: Compute mode_eval_total from the count of stocks that actually reached the mode loop (results.length * modeCount), or from (stocks.length - perStockFailures) * modeCount, and keep the denominators consistent with the per-stock gate. Document the chosen population in a comment naming the failure mode (systemic mode break diluted by wrong denominator).

nonScoring.title: Mojibake/accent folding in dedupe norm() is a fragile byte-level hack that only covers UTF-8 lead-byte artifacts, not real Unicode
nonScoring.evidence: `if (/[^\x00-\x7f]/.test(str)) { str = str.replace(/[Ã©¨ª«³²´¶¡ ¢¤]/g, function (c) { var cp = c.codePointAt(0); if (cp === 0xb3 ...) return 'o'; ... return 'e'; }); }` (lines 212-218). The character class is a hand-picked set of Latin-1 bytes plus the 0xC3 mojibake lead byte; the comment admits it maps 'the lone mojibake lead byte'.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: Real accented company names (e.g. 'Saint-Gobain', 'Münchener', 'Nestlé' stored as proper Unicode é U+00E9) are NOT in the class — only the specific mis-decoded byte sequences are handled. So genuinely-encoded foreign names and mojibake names normalize differently, meaning the same company under two encodings produces two keys and is NOT deduped, while unrelated names sharing a stripped stem ARE deduped (see A-report-modes-02). The dedupe key quality directly bounds universe integrity, and this approach silently degrades as data sources change encoding.
nonScoring.fix: Replace the byte-level hack with String.prototype.normalize('NFKD').replace(/\p{Diacritic}/gu,'') to fold all diacritics uniformly, and fix the upstream encoding so mojibake never reaches the snapshot in the first place. This makes the dedupe key encoding-independent. (Behavioral change to dedupe — pair with the keying fix in A-report-modes-02 and verify against a name-collision fixture.)

nonScoring.title: Mcap dual-slider clamp mutates the dragged slider value instead of pushing the other thumb, causing a stuck/jumpy range
nonScoring.evidence: On mcap-min input: `if (maxEl && parseFloat(input.value) > parseFloat(maxEl.value)) input.value = maxEl.value;` (line 1197); symmetric for mcap-max (line 1200). The dragged thumb is snapped back to the other thumb's value rather than the other thumb being moved.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: When the user drags min past max, min is forced back to max — the user cannot widen the window by dragging the leading thumb through the other; the range collapses to a single point and feels broken. Minor UX defect but it makes the headline mcap filter (the screener's most-used control) frustrating, contributing to the tool feeling under-finished.
nonScoring.fix: Standard two-thumb pattern: clamp by pushing the *other* thumb, or keep min<=max by setting the other slider's value, not the active one. E.g. on min overshoot set maxEl.value = input.value (and resync its label) so the window expands as expected.

nonScoring.title: Worker-pool rate-limit sleep is per-worker, not global — effective request rate is concurrency × the intended rate, defeating the anti-429 throttle
nonScoring.evidence: runWorkerPool: each worker independently does `if (myIdx + concurrency < stocks.length) await _sleep(sleepMs)` (line 2252) after every ticker. With CONCURRENCY workers each sleeping rateLimitMs between its own pulls, aggregate throughput is ~concurrency/rateLimitMs req/s. The comment at 2232 even states this: 'With 20 workers and rateLimitMs=1500ms per worker, throughput is ~13 tickers/sec.' So the 1500ms 'rate limit' is NOT a global request spacing.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: The whole point of --rate-limit ≥1500ms (documented at file top, line 19, as the defense against Yahoo 403/429 blocking) is global request spacing. Because the sleep is per-worker, raising PULL_CONCURRENCY silently multiplies the real hit-rate against Yahoo's Cloudflare edge. This is the structural mechanism behind the documented 7,210 rate-limit failures in Run #107 (referenced at line 1342) — operators lower concurrency and raise backoff to compensate, but the knob they think throttles globally does not. It caps the 14.6h pull's reliability and forces conservative concurrency.
nonScoring.fix: Introduce a single shared rate-gate (e.g. a module-level `nextSlotAt` timestamp the workers advance atomically, or a token-bucket/leaky-bucket limiter) so that the MINIMUM spacing between consecutive Yahoo requests across ALL workers is rateLimitMs — decoupled from concurrency. Then concurrency controls parallelism of in-flight requests while the gate controls issue rate. Keep the per-worker sleep removed to avoid double-counting.

nonScoring.title: Shared `idx++` work-stealing counter is technically a read-modify-write race (benign under current single-threaded event loop, fragile if any await is inserted before the increment)
nonScoring.evidence: `let idx = 0; ... const myIdx = idx++;` (lines 2236, 2239). The increment is currently synchronous and atomic on Node's single thread, so no two workers get the same index TODAY. But the pattern is only safe because nothing awaits between reading and incrementing.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: It works now, but it is a latent trap: any future refactor that makes index acquisition async (e.g. awaiting a shared rate-gate as recommended in finding 01, or a priority queue) would let two workers read the same `idx`, double-pulling one ticker and skipping another — silent universe attrition that no test would catch. Worth a one-line guard comment naming the invariant.
nonScoring.fix: Leave the logic but add a comment that index acquisition MUST stay synchronous (no await between `idx` read and increment), or switch to a shared async-safe queue (`stocks.shift()` style or an explicit cursor object) before adding any await to the acquisition path. Failure mode prevented: duplicate/skipped tickers from a future async work-steal.

nonScoring.title: price-only and full-pull scale marketCap by an FX trading-factor but never scale snap.price.regularMarketPrice on the full pull, while price-only DOES scale price — the two pull modes leave price in inconsistent currency units across refreshes
nonScoring.evidence: Price-only path multiplies BOTH price and mcap by tradingFactor: `existing.price.regularMarketPrice = q.regularMarketPrice * tradingFactor` (1606) and `existing.marketCap.value = q.marketCap * tradingFactor` (1616). But _convertSnapshotToUSD (full pull) explicitly does NOT scale price — comment at 411-414: 'We intentionally do NOT scale snap.price here … price stays in trading currency by design'. The full-pull mapper never even builds snap.price (confirmed by the NEW-2/NEW-3 note at 349-355).
nonScoring.why_it_matters: For an ADR/foreign-listed ticker, a full pull produces a snapshot whose marketCap is USD-converted but whose (absent or trading-ccy) price is unconverted, while the very next day's price-only refresh writes a USD-converted regularMarketPrice. Any consumer that reads price.regularMarketPrice (e.g. analyst-upside vs currentPrice, per-share ratios) gets a value whose currency depends on which pull mode last touched the file — a silent mixed-unit field that flips daily. This is exactly the class of FX-normalization bug that corrupts downstream ratios for non-USD names.
nonScoring.fix: Make price handling symmetric and explicit: either (a) always store price in USD in both paths (scale price by tradingFactor on full pull too, and document it), or (b) never store a converted price and have price-only also leave regularMarketPrice in trading currency, recording tradingCurrency in meta. Pick one invariant, assert it on write, and have consumers read meta.tradingCurrency to interpret price. Comment must name the failure mode: 'price-field currency drifts between full-pull and price-only refreshes'.

nonScoring.title: _priceOnlyUpdate throws AFTER mutating `existing` in memory but the snapshot is only re-persisted on success — on the mcap-floor branch it unlinks the file, otherwise a thrown price-only falls through to a full pull, but the in-memory mutation of the shared parsed object can leak if reused
nonScoring.evidence: `_priceOnlyUpdate` receives `preParsed` (the object parsed once in processOne at 1688) and mutates it in place: sets existing.meta.asOf (1562), existing.price.regularMarketPrice (1606), existing.marketCap.value (1616) BEFORE the throw points at 1583/1626. The same `_parsedSnapshot` object is then NOT re-used after a price-only failure (full pull rebuilds canonical from scratch), so today it is harmless — but the mutation-before-validation ordering is unsafe by construction.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: The price-only function partially applies a new asOf and a scaled price/mcap to the shared parsed object, then can throw (non-USD-without-fxRate at 1583, or mcap-below-floor at 1626). Because processOne discards the object on the full-pull fall-through, the corruption is currently contained, but the contract is brittle: any caller that retries with the same preParsed object, or any future code that reads _parsedSnapshot after a failed price-only, would see a half-updated snapshot with a fresh asOf but stale-source price. The fresh asOf is the dangerous part — it would make a corrupt snapshot look freshly pulled.
nonScoring.fix: Compute the new values into locals first, validate (fx-rate present, mcap ≥ floor) BEFORE any mutation of `existing`, and only then apply. Treat the parsed object as immutable until validation passes. Comment naming the failure mode: 'half-applied price-only mutation with refreshed asOf masquerading as a clean snapshot'.

nonScoring.title: Insider `shares` raw-envelope unwrap is inconsistent with _y(): reads only top-level `.raw`, so a yahoo-finance2 already-unwrapped number vs a {raw,fmt} object are handled by different code paths, and a nested/absent raw yields 0
nonScoring.evidence: Line 778: `const shares = (tx.shares && typeof tx.shares === 'object') ? tx.shares.raw : (tx.shares || 0);`. If tx.shares is an object lacking `.raw` (e.g. {value:n} shape, which yahoo-finance2 uses elsewhere — see the `_v` helpers at 963/999-1000 that check BOTH .value and .raw), `tx.shares.raw` is undefined → `netShares += (undefined || 0)` keeps 0, silently dropping the share count. The `_y` helper (484) only unwraps `.raw`; the rest of the file inconsistently checks `.value` OR `.raw`.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: Yahoo envelope shapes drift ({raw,fmt} vs {value} vs bare number). The insider-activity netShares90d / netShares signal silently zeroes out for any ticker whose insiderTransactions.shares arrives in the {value} shape, corrupting the insider-cluster signal feeding the scoring methods. It is the same {raw,fmt}-unwrapping class flagged in the audit brief, but here in a less-traveled path so it has likely gone unnoticed.
nonScoring.fix: Route every Yahoo envelope through one canonical unwrap helper that handles bare-number, {raw}, and {value} uniformly (the `_v` closures at 960 and 996 already do this — promote one to a module-level `_unwrap` and use it at line 778 and in `_y`). Failure mode prevented: silent zeroing of insider share counts on envelope-shape drift.

nonScoring.title: Insider 90-day cutoff compares a normalized millisecond timestamp against `cutoffMs` but cutoffMs is computed once at closure-eval time using Date.now() — fine — yet the `ts < cutoffMs` filter uses `!ts || ts < cutoffMs` which discards exactly-at-cutoff and treats a legitimately-zero-normalized ts as missing (off-by-one / boundary)
nonScoring.evidence: Line 743 `const cutoffMs = Date.now() - 90 * 86400 * 1000;` then line 776 `if (!ts || ts < cutoffMs) continue;`. `_normTxTs` already rejects out-of-range timestamps and returns a positive ms or null, so `!ts` for a valid ts is impossible (min valid is 2000-01-01) — that part is defensive-only. The boundary `ts < cutoffMs` excludes the transaction exactly 90 days old; minor.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: Negligible numerically (one boundary instant), but the `!ts` guard is dead given _normTxTs's contract, and the strict-less-than makes the window 89.999… days rather than inclusive 90. Worth noting only as a precision/clarity issue in a signal that is already coarse. Listed for completeness, not as a material defect.
nonScoring.fix: Use `ts == null || ts < cutoffMs` to make the missing-check explicit (ts can legitimately be a large positive number, never 0 post-normalization, so `!ts` is misleading), and decide intentionally whether the 90d edge is inclusive (`<=`). No behavior-critical change.

nonScoring.title: Hardcoded `/tmp/node_modules/yahoo-finance2` fallback require is unreachable on the Windows production box and is a fragile dev-only escape hatch
nonScoring.evidence: Line 50: `try { YahooFinance = require('/tmp/node_modules/yahoo-finance2').default; }`. The environment is Windows (`C:\Program Files\nodejs\node.exe` per constraints); `/tmp/node_modules` is a POSIX path that never resolves on the production/CI Windows runner. The comment even says 'lokale node_modules (z.B. /tmp während Dev)'.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: Harmless when the primary require succeeds, but if yahoo-finance2 is ever genuinely missing on Windows/CI, this fallback can't help — it just adds a second failing require before the FATAL exit. It is effectively dead on every real run and obscures the real failure path. Low severity, but it is the kind of dev-only artifact that should not ship.
nonScoring.fix: Drop the /tmp fallback (or gate it behind an explicit env var like YF_MODULE_PATH so it is portable). The primary `require('yahoo-finance2')` plus the existing FATAL message is sufficient.

nonScoring.title: FTS retry-on-timeout uses `e.message.includes('timeout')` which misses TimeoutError/ETIMEDOUT variants that the OTHER timeout classifier (line 1363) was specifically widened to catch
nonScoring.evidence: Line 1837: `if (attempt === 0 && (e.message.includes('timeout') || e.code === 'ECONNRESET')) continue;`. This is a plain substring check on lowercase literal 'timeout'. Contrast with quoteSummaryWithRetry's classifier (1363-1366) which was explicitly fixed (F-DP-048) to also match `e.name === 'TimeoutError'`, `e.constructor.name`, and `/timed out|ETIMEDOUT|ESOCKETTIMEDOUT|EAI_AGAIN/i`. _withAbortTimeout throws `new Error('ETIMEDOUT after …')` (line 1275) — note 'ETIMEDOUT', uppercase, no lowercase 'timeout' substring — so `.includes('timeout')` is CASE-SENSITIVE and will NOT match the wrapper's own timeout message.
nonScoring.why_it_matters: The FTS fetch is the expensive multi-call path (4 sequential HTTP requests, 60s budget).
